subject: maths
title: Compound measures — density and pressure

slides.heading: Compound measures — one quantity built from two others
slides.body: A compound measure is formed by combining two different quantities using multiplication or division. Density measures how much mass is packed into a given volume — a denser material feels heavier for the same size. Pressure measures how much force acts on a given area — a stiletto heel exerts much higher pressure than a flat shoe of the same weight because the force is concentrated on a tiny area. Both follow the same pattern: divide one quantity by another to get the compound measure.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: Density and pressure formulas
slides.formula: Density = Mass ÷ Volume (D = M/V) | Pressure = Force ÷ Area (P = F/A)
slides.formulaExplained: For density: D = M ÷ V (g/cm³ or kg/m³). Rearrange to find mass (M = D × V) or volume (V = M ÷ D). For pressure: P = F ÷ A (N/m² or N/cm²). Rearrange to find force (F = P × A) or area (A = F ÷ P). Both formulas follow the same triangle structure: the compound measure (D or P) is at the top — divide by it to isolate mass/volume or force/area. Units must be consistent throughout each calculation.
slides.whenToUse: Any question giving two of the three quantities (mass/volume/density or force/area/pressure) and asking for the third — including questions where you must rearrange to find mass, volume, force or area.
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: A piece of aluminium has a mass of 135 g and a volume of 50 cm³. Calculate its density.

steps.instruction: Check by reversing: mass = density × volume = 2.7 × 50 = 135 g ✓.

slides.conclusion: The density of the aluminium is 2.7 g/cm³.
slides.note: Numbers must differ from any question in the question bank for this subtopic.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Dividing volume by mass instead of mass by volume — e.g. density = 50 ÷ 135 ≈ 0.37 g/cm³ instead of 135 ÷ 50 = 2.7 g/cm³.
mistakes.correction: Density = Mass ÷ Volume. Mass is on top: D = M/V. If in doubt, think: a denser object has more mass in the same volume — the mass goes on top.

mistakes.mistake: Omitting or mixing up units — e.g. giving density as just '2.7' without g/cm³, or calculating in grams but stating units as kg/m³.
mistakes.correction: Always write units in the answer. Density units match the units used: mass in g and volume in cm³ gives g/cm³. Mass in kg and volume in m³ gives kg/m³.

mistakes.mistake: Rearranging the formula incorrectly when finding mass or volume — e.g. to find mass, writing M = D ÷ V instead of M = D × V.
mistakes.correction: Use the triangle: cover what you want. Cover M → D × V. Cover V → M ÷ D. Cover D → M ÷ V. Alternatively, write D = M/V and multiply both sides by V to get M = D × V.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: Density = Mass ÷ Volume. Rearranged: Mass = Density × Volume, Volume = Mass ÷ Density.
keyFacts.examTip: Draw the D|MV triangle: D on top, M and V on the bottom. Cover the unknown to read off the formula.

keyFacts.fact: Pressure = Force ÷ Area. Rearranged: Force = Pressure × Area, Area = Force ÷ Pressure.
keyFacts.examTip: Same triangle pattern as density: P on top, F and A on the bottom. Pressure increases when the same force acts on a smaller area.

keyFacts.fact: Units must match throughout: density in g/cm³ requires mass in g and volume in cm³. If units are mixed, convert first.
keyFacts.examTip: Always state units in the final answer. An answer of '9' in a density question is incomplete — it must be '9 g/cm³'.

note: keyFacts: 2-4 entries. Exam-precise language. These are what Mabel writes into her notes.
